title: Geometric estimation of NV charge-state contributions from a low-dimensional spectral representation
authors: Yuto Yamakawa, Keisuke Oshimi, Keigo Arai
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond exist in neutral (NV0) and negatively charged (NV-) states, and quantifying their respective photoluminescence (PL) contributions is important for charge-state-based measurements. Existing methods either require additional experimental control or may suffer from limited physical identifiability. Here, we introduce a geometric method for determining NV charge-state contributions from PL spectra acquired at different excitation intensities. Each spectrum is mapped into a low-dimensional space through broadband spectral weighting, where changes in the relative NV0 and NV- contributions trace a one-dimensional trajectory. Zero-phonon-line (ZPL) information from two spectra physically calibrates this trajectory, enabling the NV-PL contribution to be determined by geometric projection. Measurements on two bulk single-crystal diamond samples yielded NV- contributions in close agreement with those obtained using an independent dual-excitation reference-spectrum method, with root-mean-square errors of 1.11 and 0.31 percentage points. Under additive spectral noise, the proposed method exhibited more than an order of magnitude less variation than a ZPL-only method. Fisher-information analysis further showed that the three-dimensional CIE XYZ representation retained approximately 81% of the information about the NV- contribution available in the full spectrum. These results establish a physically calibrated approach to low-dimensional spectral estimation that combines reduced experimental overhead with robust parameter estimation and provides a general framework for spectral sensing governed by a small number of physical degrees of freedom.
summary: This work introduces a geometric method to accurately quantify the relative contributions of $	ext{NV}^0$ and $	ext{NV}^-$ charge states in diamond PL spectra. By mapping spectral variations into a low-dimensional space and using ZPL data for calibration, the authors achieve high accuracy and robustness against noise. This establishes a general, physically calibrated framework for spectral sensing in quantum materials.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of quantitatively determining the relative photoluminescence (PL) contributions of $	ext{NV}^0$ and $	ext{NV}^-$ charge states from a mixed spectrum, overcoming limitations of existing methods.
main_result: A novel geometric method using low-dimensional spectral mapping (CIE XYZ space) successfully estimates the $	ext{NV}^-$ contribution, showing agreement with independent measurements and superior noise robustness compared to ZPL-only methods.
method: The approach maps spectral variations into a low-dimensional manifold, calibrating the position along this manifold using Zero-Phonon Line (ZPL) information from two excitation intensities via geometric projection.
model_or_system: The system is Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, whose PL spectrum is a superposition of $	ext{NV}^0$ and $	ext{NV}^-$ emission. The spectral variation is modeled as a one-dimensional trajectory.
key_observables: $	ext{NV}^0$ and $	ext{NV}^-$ PL contributions, the charge-state ratio $r$, and the coordinates in the CIE XYZ color space.
important_parameters: Excitation intensity, Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and the information retention ratios (e.g., 81% for CIE XYZ).
main_assumptions: The spectral variation is assumed to lie on a low-dimensional manifold, and the method relies on physically calibrating the endpoints using ZPL features.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometric mapping of spectra to CIE XYZ vectors, the comparison of estimation results against independent methods (like Dual-Excitation Protocol), and the quantitative comparison of information retention across different spectral representations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the geometric mapping methodology using CIE XYZ coordinates, validates the method against established techniques (DEP), and concludes with rigorous information-theoretic analysis comparing the fidelity of different spectral representations.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of information theory (Fisher Information) to spectral decomposition provides a general framework for sensing, showing how much physical information can be reliably extracted from limited spectral measurements.
